processing: Orthodox Darjeeling black tea from old China bushes. The garden also makes a hand-rolled white tea.
harvest_season: The first flush in spring is what the garden is best known for; second flush muscatel lots are also sold.
appearance_dry: Small, twisted China-bush leaf in mixed olive and brown.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold in first flush, amber in second flush.
appearance_wet: Small, soft leaves in mixed green and copper.
taste_profile: Typical of China-bush Darjeeling: fine and floral in spring, with the grape-like muscatel character people look for in good second flush lots.

brewing.notes: Brewed Western-style. Small leaf gives up its flavour quickly, so keep the steep shorter than for larger clonal tea.

vintage_note: Sold by year and flush through tea merchants, not usually by the garden direct. First flush is the lot to look for, and it is best in its first year or two. Second flush keeps a little longer.
description:
Giddapahar is a small family garden about 4 km from Kurseong. The name means Eagle's Hill, and its 94 cultivated hectares sit among neighbours such as Castleton.

What sets it apart is its century-old China bushes and its modest output, around 30,000 kg a year. Small-leaved old bushes tend to give finer tea than volume, and first flush is the lot that made the garden's name. It also makes a hand-rolled white tea.

In the cup, expect what is typical of China-bush Darjeeling: delicate and floral in spring, more fruity in summer. Don't drown it in boiling water or leave it long; spring lots go sharp quickly.

The tea reaches drinkers through merchants, so the lot, year and flush on the label are what to check. If you are near Kurseong, the same hill holds the Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose Museum, in the house where Bose was held under house arrest in 1936.
history:
The garden was established in 1881 and has stayed with the Shaw family ever since, now in its fourth generation. Brothers Sudhansu and Himangsu Shaw run it.

That unbroken family ownership is unusual in a district whose gardens mostly began under British planters and changed hands many times.
